title: Beowulf
description: The greatest surviving poem in Old English: a heroic epic of 3,182 alliterative lines recounting the deeds of the Geatish hero Beowulf against the monster Grendel, Grendel's mother, and, fifty years later, a dragon. It combines the legendary history of Scandinavia with a profound Christian meditation on heroism, mortality, and the limits of earthly glory.
plot_or_argument: The young hero Beowulf sails from Geatland to Denmark to rid King Hrothgar's hall Heorot of the man-eating monster Grendel, whom he defeats in a night combat; he then tracks Grendel's mother to her underwater lair and slays her. Rewarded and honoured, he returns home and eventually rules the Geats for fifty years, until a dragon, enraged by the theft of a cup from its hoard, ravages his kingdom; the aged king kills the dragon but dies of his wounds, and the poem ends with his funeral pyre and the foreboding of his people's doom.
narrative_structure: A bipartite structure (youthful Danish adventures; old age and the dragon) framed by the funerals of Scyld Scefing and Beowulf; interlaced with digressions — the Finnsburh episode, the Sigmund lay, the Swedish-Geatish wars, and the 'Lay of the Last Survivor' — that mirror and darken the main action.
principal_characters: Beowulf, Hrothgar, Grendel, Grendel's mother, the dragon, Wiglaf, Hygelac, Unferth, Wealhtheow, Scyld Scefing
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre: four stresses per line divided by a caesura; formulaic diction, kennings, and variation throughout.
historical_context: Composed somewhere between the age of Bede and the eve of the Conquest, and copied c. 1000 in the Nowell Codex (British Library, Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv); its heroes belong to sixth-century Scandinavia (Hygelac's raid on Frisia, c. 521, is historical), while its audience was Christian Anglo-Saxon England.
literary_significance: The foundational epic of English literature; the first extended poetic masterpiece in any Germanic vernacular; a touchstone for subsequent English poetry (Tolkien, Auden, Heaney) and for the study of Germanic legend.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; authorship_status reflects scholarly consensus. Ascribed to no known poet.
bibliographical_notes: Nowell Codex, British Library, Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv, fols. 132-201v; damaged in the Cotton fire of 1731; first printed by Grímur Jónsson Thorkelin (1815).

title: The Wanderer
description: An elegy of 115 lines in which a solitary exile, deprived of lord and hall, meditates on the transience of earthly joy and arrives at a hard-won Christian consolation. One of the most admired poems in the Exeter Book and the supreme statement of the Old English ubi sunt theme.
plot_or_argument: The speaker, an 'eardstapa' (earth-stepper) wandering the frozen seas since the death of his lord, remembers the lost joys of the hall and laments the ruin of the world's splendour ('Where is the horse? Where is the young warrior?'); the poem closes with the famous gnomic consolation that a wise man keeps faith and seeks mercy from the Father in heaven, where all stability dwells.
narrative_structure: A movement from personal lament through the ubi sunt catalogue of vanished glories to a generalizing wisdom passage and a prayerful conclusion; framed by the figure of the wise man who speaks little and reflects much.
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre with the formulaic diction of the heroic tradition, turned to meditative ends.
historical_context: Preserved only in the Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 76v-78r), a late tenth-century anthology; the poem's heroic nostalgia is often read against the upheavals of the Viking age, though its date of composition is unknown.
literary_significance: The classic Old English elegy; a locus classicus for the ubi sunt topos and for the Christian reframing of the heroic ethos.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501.

title: The Seafarer
description: An elegy of 124 lines spoken by a veteran seafarer who describes the hardship and the irresistible pull of the sea voyage, then allegorizes it as the soul's pilgrimage away from the world toward its heavenly home.
plot_or_argument: The speaker recounts winters of cold watch on the ice-cold sea, hunger, and isolation, yet declares that the sea calls him again; earthly joys, lords, and kingdoms all pass, and the wise man sets his hope on the eternal home where all things endure — the journey of the seafarer becoming a figure for the Christian's exile in the world.
narrative_structure: Two movements: a first-person account of seafaring hardship and longing, and a homiletic second half that interprets the voyage allegorically (peregrinatio pro amore Dei); the transition between them is a crux of interpretation.
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre; vivid winter seascape imagery rare in the corpus.
historical_context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; influenced by the penitential and pilgrimage traditions (the phrase 'dryhtnes dreamas' has suggested the peregrinus ideal of Irish and Anglo-Saxon monasticism).
literary_significance: Alongside The Wanderer, the great poem of Old English exile; its seascape and spiritual allegory influenced Pound's 'The Seafarer' and much modern poetry.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 81b-83a.

title: The Wife's Lament
description: An elegy of 53 lines, unique in the corpus for its sustained female voice: a woman separated from her lord laments her exile in an earth-cave beneath an oak tree and curses the man responsible for her misery.
plot_or_argument: The speaker tells how her lord departed over the sea, how his kin plotted against them, and how she was banished to a desolate dwelling in the wilderness, where she sits weeping through the long days; she ends by wishing upon her beloved the sorrow of one who sits apart, remembering a happier home.
narrative_structure: A first-person lament moving from past happiness through separation and exile to a bitter wish against the absent beloved; the obscurity of the situation (which lord, which feud) is itself part of the poem's design.
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre; unusually personal and passionate diction.
historical_context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; the poem has been read as autobiography, as allegory (the Church or the soul lamenting Christ), and as a riddle-like exercise — a famous crux of Old English scholarship.
literary_significance: The first sustained female voice in English poetry and a key text for feminist criticism of the period.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 115a-115b.

title: Wulf and Eadwacer
description: A famously enigmatic poem of 19 lines in which a woman cries out against the separation of 'Wulf' from herself and 'Eadwacer', their child; its refrain — 'Ungelice is us' ('It is different for us') — and its riddling situation have made it the most debated short poem in Old English.
plot_or_argument: The speaker laments that her people will take Wulf if he comes to them ('they will receive him if he comes in a band'), that their child is being carried off to the woods, and that the embrace she once knew is gone; the poem closes on the refrain and the image of Wulf carrying their whelp to the wood.
narrative_structure: A compressed dramatic monologue of seven half-stanzas bound by a refrain, preserving an otherwise lost story (perhaps from the cycle of Wulf and Eadwacer, or a riddle, or an allegory).
literary_form: elegiac dramatic monologue in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre with a refrain; the irregular lineation has suggested an underlying strophic form.
historical_context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; interpretations range from heroic legend to riddle to Christian allegory.
literary_significance: The most mysterious and most modern-sounding of the Exeter Book poems; a touchstone for theories of the Old English lyric.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 100b-101a.

title: The Husband's Message
description: An elegiac poem of 54 lines in which a wooden rune-stave, carved with a message, speaks on behalf of an exiled lord to the woman he loves, recalling their former vows and summoning her to join him across the sea.
plot_or_argument: The stave tells how its lord was forced into exile by a feud, how he longs for his lady, and how he now sends word that he has wealth and a hall prepared for her; the poem closes with a runic passage (often solved as 'sige', 'rad', and other rune-names) promising their reunion and the renewal of their vows.
narrative_structure: A speaking object (prosopopoeia) delivers the lord's message; the closing runic riddle has prompted attempts to read the poem as part of a composite sequence with the riddles that follow it in the manuscript.
principal_characters: the rune-stave (speaker); the lord; the lady
historical_context: Preserved in the Exeter Book, following the riddles; often paired with The Wife's Lament as complementary perspectives on exile and separated love.
literary_significance: An early and sophisticated use of the speaking-object device and of runic writing as poetic material.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 123a-123b.

title: The Ruin
description: A fragmentary elegy (about 49 lines, damaged by burning of the manuscript leaf) describing the ruins of a great stone city — hot springs, halls, and baths that are almost certainly Roman Bath — and meditating on the fall of its builders.
plot_or_argument: The speaker marvels at 'enta geweorc' (the work of giants): broken walls, fallen roofs, and the hot baths where once many men bathed in comfort; the city's warriors are dead, its halls decayed, and the poem closes with the reflection that a hundred generations have passed since its glory.
narrative_structure: A description of ruins moving from sensory observation to historical meditation, in the ubi sunt mode.
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre; the text is incomplete through fire damage.
historical_context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; the identification with Roman Bath is standard.
literary_significance: The earliest ruin-poem in English, anticipating the ruin tradition of the eighteenth century; a haunting witness to Anglo-Saxon wonder at Roman remains.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 123b-124b (badly damaged).

title: Deor
description: A poem of 42 lines spoken by a displaced court poet, Deor, who consoles himself with a catalogue of legendary woes — Weland's captivity, Beadohild's pregnancy, Mæðhild's grief, Theodoric's exile, Eormanric's tyranny — each closed by the refrain 'Þæs ofereode, þisses swa mæg' ('That passed over, so may this').
plot_or_argument: Deor, supplanted in his lord's favour by a rival scop named Heorrenda, lists the legendary sorrows that came to an end and applies the refrain to his own case, ending with a brief, ambiguous self-identification as the once-favoured poet of the Heodenings.
narrative_structure: Five legendary exempla framed by the refrain, followed by the poet's personal application; the refrain is the earliest in English poetry.
principal_characters: Deor (speaker); Weland; Beadohild; Mæðhild; Theodoric; Eormanric; Heorrenda
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre with a six-part strophic structure marked by the refrain.
historical_context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; its allusions are the earliest English witnesses to the legends of Weland the smith and Eormanric the Goth.
literary_significance: A rare glimpse of the court poet's self-consciousness and of the consolation-structure that underlies the Old English elegies.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; the speaker's name is part of the fiction.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fol. 100a-100b.

title: Widsith
description: A catalogue-poem of 143 lines spoken by the scop Widsith, who boasts of the lands, kings, and tribes he has visited — a thula (name-list) that preserves the oldest stratum of Germanic heroic legend in English, from Eormanric the Goth to Hrothgar of the Danes.
plot_or_argument: Widsith introduces himself as a poet of the Myrgings, recounts the lords he has served (Eormanric, Eadgils, Ælfwine, Hrothgar and Hrothwulf among dozens), and ends with a professional credo on the value of the scop, who wanders among peoples earning praise and treasure with his songs.
narrative_structure: Three thulas (catalogues of kings, tribes, and personal patrons) framed by first-person narrative and a gnomic coda on the poet's craft.
principal_characters: Widsith (speaker); Eormanric; Hrothgar; Hrothwulf; Eadgils; Ælfwine; Offa; Ealhhild
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre of the older, stichic kind.
historical_context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; its name-lists reach back to the fourth-century Gothic world and have been central to reconstructing Germanic heroic legend.
literary_significance: The earliest map of Germanic heroic geography in English; a key text for the prehistory of Beowulf's world.
bibliographical_notes: Exeter Book, Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501, fols. 84b-87a.

title: The Battle of Maldon
description: A fragmentary poem of 325 lines commemorating the battle of Maldon (10 or 11 August 991), in which Ealdorman Byrhtnoth of Essex and his retinue fought a Viking army at the causeway of the Blackwater and were destroyed; the poem is the last great expression of the heroic code, celebrating loyalty unto death.
plot_or_argument: Byrhtnoth arrays his levies against the Vikings on the tidal causeway of the Pante; he refuses tribute, and when the Vikings ask passage he grants it 'for his ofermod' (overconfidence) — the poem's great crux — drawing up for battle on the shore. After Byrhtnoth falls, a series of retainers make speeches vowing to avenge him or die beside him, and the poem breaks off in the midst of the last stand.
narrative_structure: A single continuous battle-narrative built from speeches: the Viking messenger's demand, Byrhtnoth's reply, the combat, and the laddered sequence of retainers' vows (Ælfwine, Offa, Leofsunu, Dunnere, Byrhtwold — 'will shall be the harder, heart the keener').
principal_characters: Byrhtnoth; Wulfstan; Ælfhere; Maccus; Offa; Ælfwine; Leofsunu; Dunnere; Byrhtwold; Godric (the betrayer)
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre of the classical kind, with sustained martial diction.
historical_context: The battle is recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle s.a. 991 and in the Vita Oswaldi; the poem survives only in an early eighteenth-century transcript of Cotton MS Otho A.xii, destroyed in the Cotton fire of 1731. The tribute of 10,000 pounds paid after the battle began the Danegeld payments.
literary_significance: The fullest poetic statement of the comitatus ethic of loyalty unto death; Byrhtwold's speech is among the most quoted passages of Old English verse.
attribution_notes: Anonymous; the opening and closing of the poem are lost with the manuscript.
bibliographical_notes: Formerly London, British Library, Cotton MS Otho A.xii (destroyed 1731); preserved in transcripts (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Rawlinson B.203).

title: The Battle of Brunanburh
description: A panegyric of 73 lines, entered in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for the year 937, celebrating the crushing victory of King Æthelstan and his brother Edmund over a coalition of Scots, Strathclyde Britons, and Dublin Norsemen led by Constantine and Anlaf (Olaf) Guthfrithson. The greatest of the Chronicle's poems, composed in the full heroic manner.
plot_or_argument: The poem exults in the day-long battle — 'never was greater slaughter in this island' — as the West Saxons and Mercians pursue the fleeing allies; Constantine, his son slain, and Anlaf flee to their ships, and the victors return to Wessex leaving the battlefield to the carrion beasts, the raven, eagle, and wolf.
narrative_structure: A compact celebration in the heroic mode: the boast of victory, the pursuit, the flight of the kings, and the 'beasts of battle' topos, with a closing return to the annalistic frame.
principal_characters: Æthelstan; Edmund; Constantine of Scotland; Anlaf Guthfrithson
literary_form: battle poetry (chronicle poem) in alliterative verse
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre; dense use of kennings and the beasts-of-battle formula.
historical_context: The battle of Brunanburh (937), the greatest English victory of the tenth century, secured Æthelstan's supremacy in Britain; the poem is preserved in four manuscripts of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.
literary_significance: The masterpiece of late heroic panegyric; Tennyson's translation (1880) is a landmark of Victorian medievalism.
bibliographical_notes: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle MSS A, B, C, D, s.a. 937.

title: The Finnsburh Fragment
manuscript_date: lost; preserved in an early eighteenth-century transcript
description: A fragment of about 48 lines of an older heroic lay describing the night attack on the hall of Finn, king of the Frisians, in which the Danish prince Hnæf and his men defend the doors for five days. The story — later told allusively in Beowulf's 'Finnsburg episode' — is one of the great Germanic tales of feud and loyalty.
plot_or_argument: A watchman sees the gleam of weapons as Finn's men attack the hall by night; Hnæf's Danes hold the doors, and the fight lasts five days without a man falling, until the fragment breaks off. The fuller story, reconstructed from Beowulf and other sources, involves the peace-pledge of Hildeburh, the death of Hnæf and Finn's son, and Finn's eventual slaying by the Danes.
narrative_structure: A single vivid scene of hall-fighting, extended by speeches (the door-defenders Garulf and Guðere, the veteran Sigeferth); the poem's brevity and compression suggest the style of the older lays behind Beowulf.
principal_characters: Hnæf; Finn; Hildeburh; Hengest; Sigeferth; Garulf; Guðlaf; Ordlaf
meter_and_prosody: Alliterative accentual metre of an archaic, compressed kind.
historical_context: The story belongs to the fifth-century Germanic migrations; the text survives only in the transcript made by George Hickes for his Thesaurus (1705) of a manuscript leaf (Lambeth Palace MS 487) now lost.
literary_significance: The sole surviving example, alongside Beowulf, of the heroic hall-fight; indispensable for reconstructing the legend and the older lay tradition.
bibliographical_notes: Hickes's transcript (1705) of a lost Lambeth Palace manuscript leaf.

title: Waldere
description: Two fragments (about 63 lines) of an Old English heroic poem on Walter of Aquitaine, the legend known fully from the tenth-century Latin Waltharius: the hostage Walter, escaped with his beloved Hildegyth, is overtaken by the Burgundian king Guthhere (Gunther) and refuses to surrender his treasure and his bride.
plot_or_argument: In the first fragment, Hildegyth urges Walter to fight, praising his sword Mimming and the treasures of the world's kings; in the second, a warrior (perhaps Guthhere or Hagen) taunts Walter over the shield and byrnie taken from Weland's workshop, and Walter answers boastfully that the man who comes for the gold shall have battle. The fragments preserve the defiant speech-exchange before the single combats of the fuller legend.
narrative_structure: A dialogue of challenge and defiance between two (or three) warriors, in the heroic flyting mode.
principal_characters: Waldere (Walter); Hildegyth; Guthhere; Hagen (in the underlying legend); Weland (as maker of the arms)
historical_context: The legend of Walter of Aquitaine, rooted in fifth-century events, circulated across the Germanic world (Waltharius, the Nibelung tradition); the English fragments were discovered in 1860 in the Royal Library, Copenhagen, used as binding material.
literary_significance: The English witness to one of the great heroic legends of the Middle Ages, bridging the worlds of Beowulf and the continental epics.
bibliographical_notes: Copenhagen, Royal Library, fragments Ny kgl. Saml. 167b.

title: Cædmon's Hymn
manuscript_date: margins of eighth-century manuscripts of Bede
description: A nine-line praise poem to God the Creator, composed, according to Bede's Historia ecclesiastica (IV.24), by the illiterate cowherd Cædmon after a dream in which he was commanded to sing of the beginning of created things. It is the earliest datable poem in Old English.
plot_or_argument: The poem praises the heavenly Father, the measurer of fate, who established the beginning of every wonder: first he created heaven as a roof for the children of men, then the middle-earth, the guardian of mankind made the earth for men. (This is the traditional five-line paraphrase; the text runs to nine lines with epithets varying by version.)
narrative_structure: A single doxological period: address, epithets of God, and the two works of creation (heaven, earth).
meter_and_prosody: Nine lines of alliterative accentual metre, with formulaic epithets ('heofonrices weard', 'moncynnes weard').
historical_context: Composed c. 657–680 at Whitby under Abbess Hild; Bede gives a Latin paraphrase and says the vernacular text was preserved; it survives in Old English in the margins and endleaves of some twenty-one manuscripts of the Historia, the earliest (the 'Moore Bede') datable to 737.
literary_significance: The earliest surviving English poem and the foundation of the English religious poetic tradition.
attribution_notes: Traditionally attributed to Cædmon on Bede's authority; the extant Old English texts are translations back from oral memory of the original, which Bede knew only in paraphrase.
bibliographical_notes: Earliest Old English text: Cambridge, University Library, Kk.5.16 ('Moore Bede', 737); Northumbrian and West Saxon recensions.
